notes: Do not plant out until all frost risk has passed. Needs warm nights.
Very frost-sensitive. Can direct sow outdoors once soil is warm.
Cool-season crop. Bolts in high summer heat. Succession sow every 3 weeks.
Direct sow only – dislikes root disturbance. Thin to 5cm spacing.
Cool-season. Sow early — peas prefer cool root runs.
Needs a warm long summer. Best in blocks for wind pollination.
Bolts quickly in heat. Best as a spring or autumn crop.
Very hardy. Flavour improves after frost. Cut-and-come-again.
Direct sow. Each 'seed' is actually a cluster of seeds — thin to 10cm.
Long-season crop. Sets (small bulbs) are a quicker alternative to seed.
Needs a wigwam or trellis. Frost-sensitive — don't plant out until all risk has passed.
Prolific producer. Pick regularly to keep plants cropping.
Needs a very long warm season. Best grown under glass or polytunnel in the UK.
Needs high germination heat. Start very early indoors. Greenhouse gives best results.
Very heat-demanding. In cool climates, greenhouse is virtually essential.
Winter staple. Plant in dibbed holes — don't backfill, just water in.
Long-season brassica. Needs firm soil — stake in exposed sites. Improves after frost.
Spring, summer and winter varieties available. Net against cabbage white butterfly.
Blanch the curds by folding outer leaves over once they appear.
Cut the central head to promote side shoots for extended harvest.
Overwinters outdoors. Harvested in late winter–spring — a true hungry gap filler.
Very slow to germinate — use fresh seed each year. Sweetens after frost.
Hardy winter root. Sow in June. Can leave in ground until needed.
Needs a long season. Start early under cover. Remove lower leaves in summer.
Fastest crop in the garden. Succession sow every 2 weeks for continuous supply.
Cut-and-come-again. Tolerates light frost — productive spring through autumn.
Bolts in heat. Best as spring or autumn crop. Sow mid-summer for autumn harvest.
Succession sow every 3 weeks for continuous supply. Very quick turnaround.
Needs long hot summers. Greenhouse strongly recommended in the UK.
Autumn sow (Oct–Nov) overwinters as young plants. Hardy — tolerates hard frosts. Pinch out blackfly-prone tips in spring.
Spring sow (Feb–Mar) for June–July harvest. Hardy enough to sow direct as soon as soil is workable.
Plant individual cloves (not seed) Oct–Nov, pointy end up, 5cm deep. Needs cold period to vernalise. Harvest when lower leaves yellow.
Sow outdoors Jul–Aug, transplant Sep–Oct, harvest Feb–May. Overwinters as young plant. Net against cabbage white butterfly.
Harvest small (golf ball size) for best flavour. Succession sow every 3 weeks Mar–Jun.
Pull young for tender salad turnips or leave to swell for mash. Succession sow for continuous supply.
Needs plenty of space and rich soil. Cure in sun after harvest to harden skins for storage.
Greenhouse varieties crop far more reliably in the UK. Train up a vertical support. Pick regularly to keep plants fruiting.
Chit tubers in egg boxes 4–6 weeks before planting. Plant Feb–early Mar, 10cm deep. Earth up as shoots emerge. New potatoes — dig when flowers open.
Plant Mar–Apr, 15cm deep, 40cm apart. Earth up regularly. Leave foliage to die back before harvesting. Store in paper sacks in a cool dark frost-free place.
Perennial — plant 1-year-old crowns for quickest results. No picking for the first 2 years. Establishes in a permanent bed; harvest spears 6–8 weeks in spring from year 3.
Tiny seeds — surface sow, don't cover. Needs consistent moisture throughout. Self-blanching varieties are easiest; trench celery has better flavour.
Succession sow every 3 weeks Mar–Aug. Bolts quickly in summer heat — choose slow-bolt varieties. Autumn sowings are peppery and flavourful. Pick young leaves for salad.
Large perennial — plant as offsets (suckers) from established plants for first-year harvest. Harvest buds before scales open. Protect crowns with straw in winter.
Needs a long warm season. Start indoors Apr–May, plant out after last frost. Cure at room temp for 10 days after harvest to harden skin for long storage.
Grow from slips (rooted cuttings from a tuber). Needs warm soil above 15°C consistently. Greenhouse essential in the UK. Harvest before first frost; cure in warmth before storing.
Plant tubers 10–15cm deep, Feb–Mar. Extremely vigorous — grow in a dedicated bed. Tall plants provide windbreak. Harvest tubers after foliage dies back; leave some in ground to regrow.
Direct sow Mar–Apr — dislikes root disturbance. Deep, stone-free soil essential. Frost sweetens the roots. Leave in ground until needed; edible shoots in spring.
Grow from root cuttings (thongs) planted Feb–Mar at 45°. Extremely invasive perennial — contain in a bucket sunk in the ground. Harvest in autumn; lift all roots or regrowth is vigorous.
Sow Jun–Jul for autumn/winter harvest. For chicory chicons: lift roots in autumn, pot in compost, exclude light at 10–18°C for 3–4 weeks. Radicchio hearts in cold weather.
Italian winter kale with distinctive dark, crinkled leaves. Sow Mar–May, harvest Nov through Mar. Frost improves flavour. Pick from the bottom up, leaving growing tip intact.
Southern US staple, excellent in the UK as a cold-hardy leafy green. Cut-and-come-again. More heat-tolerant than kale; harvest leaves before they become tough.
Fast-growing. Succession sow every 2–3 weeks for continuous supply. Bolts quickly in summer heat — favour early spring and autumn sowings. Peppery flavour intensifies with age.
Watercress substitute for garden beds — no running water needed. Hardy; sow in August for winter salads under cover. Peppery; pick young leaves.
Sow direct May–Jun in warm soil. Harvest pods when plump and bright green — they go from perfect to over-ripe quickly. Must be boiled before eating; don't eat raw.
Plant sets Oct–Nov, 2cm deep, 15cm apart. Each set multiplies into a cluster. Longer-storing and milder than onions. Harvest when foliage yellows; dry thoroughly before storing.
Needs a longer, warmer season than runner beans. Greenhouse gives reliable crops in the UK. Harvest pods when beans feel plump but before they harden. Climbing varieties need support.
Must grow at least two plants for fruit set (cross-pollination required). Harvest when husk splits or turns papery. Treat like tomatoes for growing conditions.
Requires a long warm growing season — works best in warm UK summers or under cover. Sow direct in warm soil Apr–May. Harvest green pods for fresh eating or leave to dry fully.
Heated propagator essential for germination. Greenhouse or polytunnel required for reliable UK production. Harvest pods at 5–8cm — they toughen quickly if left longer.
Trailing squash — allow 2–3m space or train vertically. Harvest when skin is golden-yellow and hard. Internal flesh separates into spaghetti-like strands when baked.
Sow Aug–Sep for Dec–Mar harvest. Use cold-hardy varieties (Little Gem, Arctic King, Winter Density). Under cloches or cold frame to prevent frost damage to outer leaves.
Large Japanese radish — can reach 50cm+ long. Sow direct Apr–Aug. Bolt-prone if sown too early. Autumn sowings (Jul–Aug) give roots up to 60cm long. Grate fresh or use in stews.
